questions.stem: Which four factors determine the size of a population?

options.text: Birth rate, death rate, immigration, and emigration

questions.explanation: Population size is determined by birth rate (increases population), death rate (decreases population), immigration (organisms moving in), and emigration (organisms moving out).

options.text: The total number of species in an ecosystem
The rate at which a population grows
The maximum population size that an environment can sustain
The minimum number of organisms needed to survive

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size that an environment can sustainably support with available resources. When a population reaches carrying capacity, birth rate roughly equals death rate and population growth levels off.

questions.stem: What shape does a population growth curve typically show when resources are limited?
questions.explanation: When resources are limited, a population typically shows an S-shaped (sigmoidal) growth curve. Growth starts slowly, then increases rapidly, and finally levels off as the population approaches the carrying capacity of the environment.

questions.stem: In a predator-prey relationship, what typically happens when the prey population increases?

options.text: The predator population stays the same
The predator population increases after a time lag

questions.explanation: When prey numbers increase, more food is available for predators, so predator numbers increase after a time lag. The predator population increase then causes the prey population to decline, creating cyclical fluctuations.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a density-dependent limiting factor?
questions.explanation: Competition for food is density-dependent because its effect increases as population density increases. More individuals means more competition for limited resources. Volcanic eruptions, floods, and wildfires are density-independent factors.

options.text: Competition between members of different species
Competition between members of the same species

questions.explanation: Interspecific competition is competition between members of different species for the same resources, such as food, light, or space. Competition between members of the same species is called intraspecific competition.

questions.stem: What happens to a population that exceeds its carrying capacity?

options.text: It adapts instantly to the new conditions
The death rate increases and the population declines back towards carrying capacity
The carrying capacity increases to match the population

questions.explanation: When a population exceeds carrying capacity, resources become scarce, leading to increased competition, starvation, and disease. The death rate increases and the population declines back towards or below the carrying capacity.
